title: Experimental, Wankel-Powered Mercedes-Benz C111-II Headed to Auction

body_markdown:
Mercedes-Benz built 17 units of the forward-thinking C111 to test new technologies, and only 13 of those remain. None have ever been offered for sale to the public; they’re all still owned by the brand, so the only way to put one in your garage has been to buy a scale model. That will change at Retromobile 2027: RM Sotheby’s will offer a Mercedes-Benz C111 to private buyers for the first time.


Designed as a rolling laboratory with supercar proportions,[the C111](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/even-after-55-years-mercedes-wankel-powered-c111-is-still-a-marvel/) made its debut at the 1969 Frankfurt auto show with gullwing doors inspired by the 300SL, wedge-shaped styling, and composite body panels. It was powered by a futuristic, three-rotor Wankel engine linked to a five-speed manual transmission. Many carmakers believed that the rotary engine[had a tremendous amount of potential](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/that-time-citroen-built-and-tested-a-helicopter-with-twin-rotor-wankel-power/) during the late 1960s, and Mercedes-Benz was determined to stay ahead of its rivals by solving the Wankel’s problems.


Beyond the drivetrain, the C111 stood out as one of the first cars designed with the help of a computer. Mercedes-Benz developed the model using a software called Elasto-Static Elements-Method (ESEM) that it created in-house to digitally calculate dynamic loads, and it proudly referred to the C111 as “the car that came from the computer.” Bruno Sacco was put in charge of the styling.


Mercedes-Benz started testing the C111 immediately after its debut, and it even let a handful of journalists take a ride in one. Early tests were positive, and period road-testers praised the C111’s strong performance, excellent handling, and safe, predictable brakes.

Executives considered giving the C111 the proverbial green light for production, but the coupe never saw the light at the end of a production line. Instead, the feedback gathered was used to develop an even more powerful model called C111-II that made its debut at the 1970 Geneva auto show. The second-generation model was fitted with a 350-horsepower, four-rotor Wankel engine, and it featured several updates such as a bigger windshield, styling changes on both ends, and a full-length center console.


Demand for the C111-II was strong. Enthusiasts asked Mercedes-Benz how to buy one without having driven it, and with no idea of how much it would cost. And yet, the coupe remained at the prototype stage. Part of the problem stemmed from the fact that the C111-II couldn’t pass then-looming safety and emissions regulations in the United States, which would have been a major market. Retrofitting, say, a straight-six wasn’t possible, because the entire car was designed around a compact, four-rotor Wankel engine.


All told, Mercedes-Benz built nine units of the C111 and eight units of the C111-II. The project didn’t end there: Engineers later gave up on Wankel technology and fitted the C111-III and the C111-IV with[turbodiesel engines](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/7-diesel-powered-sports-car-concepts-that-never-made-it/) , but none reached production.


Shown here, the Mercedes-Benz C111-II that RM Sotheby’s[will auction off](https://rmsothebys.com/auctions/pa27/lots/r0023-1970-mercedesbenz-c-111ii) during its Retromobile 2027 sale was assigned chassis number 33. It was built from March to August of 1970, and it’s finished in a shade of orange called Weißherbst with a black and houndstooth interior. Engineers used it to test numerous functions and parameters, including ensuring that the sill-mounted fuel tanks drained at even levels and checking how hot the trunk got in normal operating conditions. You’re on the wrong track if you’re picturing the C111-II carrying around a small trailer’s worth of measuring equipment: Mercedes-Benz merely put a stick of butter in the trunk and drove around. If the butter melted, the trunk got too hot. If it didn’t melt, the trunk’s temperature was acceptable.

Chassis number 33 was also used for promotional purposes throughout the 1970s, and it joined Mercedes-Benz’s private collection of cars in September 1975. It has since been displayed in museums and collections in Germany and abroad. Keeping a dauntingly experimental car road-worthy was easier said than done, however, so the car remained in non-running condition for several years.


Mercedes-Benz Classic got chassis number 33 running in the early 2020s and brought it to the 2024 edition of the Pebble Beach Concours d’Elegance, among other international events. Fast-forward to the present, and chassis number 33 is offered in running and driving condition with two sets of wheels (including one used for high-speed testing in the 1970s) and a modern on-board fire suppression system in the trunk. Its odometer shows approximately 24,800 kilometers, which represents roughly 15,400 miles.


RM Sotheby’s didn’t provide a pre-auction estimate, but it pegs the C111-II’s value at over $27 million. The proceeds from the sale will help Mercedes-Benz overhaul its museum in Stuttgart, Germany. Don’t expect the German company to sell another C111 the next time it needs money: Mercedes-Benz is contractually committed not to offer another C111 for sale for at least 25 years.
